notes:
Let me read the main texts I already have.I found James 2 notes from these sources: Enduring Word (Guzik), Ellicott, Gill, the Pulpit Commentary, Wesley's Notes, Precept Austin, Matthew Henry, Clarke, Constable, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB), the Church Pulpit Commentary and Maclaren. The research tool hit its usage limit before I could open any Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran-site, Bible Odyssey, NET Bible or prosperity-teaching pages. Those parts are missing, not left out on purpose. Also, some sources only gave me excerpts, so a few verses have thin notes.

## Part 1: Verse-by-verse (the traditional reading)

**v. 1**
- "Lord of glory" is a strong title for Jesus. Guzik cites Moffatt: Christ is the full showing of God's presence, which Jews called the *shekinah*. Because the Lord shows no favouritism, his people shouldn't either. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-2/
- The name "brothers" shows Christians are equal, and that is the reason for the command. Don't honour anyone just for being rich, or look down on anyone just for being poor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/james/2.htm
- Clarke thinks the verse could be read as a question: "Do you claim the faith of Christ while favouring people?" https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/james-2.html
- The Pulpit Commentary agrees both readings (a command or a question) are possible. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/james/2-1.htm
- Gill: believers are children of one Father and one in Christ, rich or poor. The glory of Christ belongs to all of them equally. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-2.html

**v. 2**
- The Greek word for "meeting" is literally "synagogue." Ellicott says this is the only place in the New Testament where it is used for a Christian gathering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/james-2.html
- Guzik takes this as a sign the church was still mostly Jewish when James wrote. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-2/
- Gill says some think a law court is meant here (compare v. 6), not a worship service. He quotes a Jewish rule that the two sides in a court case should be dressed alike. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-2.html
- The Pulpit Commentary: the fuss made over a rich visitor suggests rich people were unusual in early congregations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/2.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: proper respect isn't condemned. What is condemned is fawning over wealth and success, "some new golden calf." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/james-2.html
- The Pulpit Commentary gives modern examples: special pews for the lord of the manor, and preachers who go easy on influential families. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/james-2.html

**v. 4**
- Wesley: you are reasoning badly and so judging wrongly, because fine clothes prove nothing about a person's worth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/james/2.htm
- Gill: they were telling rich and poor apart by an evil way of thinking, assuming one is better than the other. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/2.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary, citing Farrar, says this is doubt: acting as if Christ had never promised his kingdom to the poor. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/james-2.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik: God doesn't favour poverty as such. The poor simply have fewer obstacles to trusting God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-2/
- Precept Austin: James isn't praising poverty. He is exposing how foolish it is to judge by the world's standards. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james-2-commentary
- For how the traditions differ on the idea of God's choosing here, see Part 2.

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: "dishonoured" refers back to the seating in vv. 2–3. This was a class of rich people, not every rich person. He adds that Roman courts in the provinces were often corrupt and that legal fees shut out the poor. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/james-2.html
- Wesley: the rich oppressed people by open violence, and dragged them to court under cover of law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/james/2.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary compares this to Saul dragging believers off to prison (Acts 8:3). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/2.htm
- Gill: this doesn't apply to all rich men, and it doesn't cancel proper social order. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-2.html
- Precept Austin: the readers were flattering Christ's enemies while despising the very people God had chosen. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james-2-commentary

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: most commentators take "the noble name" to mean Christ's name, the name the readers were baptised into. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/2.htm
- Wesley: it means the name of God and of Christ. James mainly has rich pagans in mind, though Wesley asks whether so-called Christians are any better. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/james/2.htm

**v. 8**
- Gill: it is called "royal" because it is the law of the King of kings and the chief of laws. The Syriac translation reads "the law of God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/2.htm
- Wesley: it is the highest law of the great King, which is love to everyone, poor as well as rich. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/james/2.htm
- Ellicott hears a touch of irony: "if you really are keeping the law, as you claim..." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/2.htm
- Precept Austin reads the verse as a sharp rebuke, not praise. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james-2-commentary
- The Pulpit Commentary gives two views. Huther thinks James is answering readers who used the love command to excuse favouring the rich. Alford thinks James is simply guarding his own argument from being misread. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/2.htm

**v. 9**
- Gill describes the law acting like a court case: it accuses, proves, convicts and condemns. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/2.htm
- Wesley cross-references Exodus 23:3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/james/2.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: the law is like a chain that snaps if one link breaks. But not all sins are equal in their effect or their punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/2.htm
- Gill: sins are not all equal (against the Stoics). Even so, no one can be justified by obeying the law imperfectly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-2.html
- Constable: "guilty of all" means you have broken God's law, not that you have broken every commandment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/james-2.html
- Wesley: you are as liable to condemnation as if you had broken every point. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/james/2.htm

**v. 11**
- Wesley: the same authority stands behind every command. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/james/2.htm
- Matthew Henry: people are strict about some sins and relaxed about others. Someone who looks to the Lawgiver's authority will respect all of his commands. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jam/Jam_002.cfm
- Precept Austin: putting favouritism next to adultery and murder shows how serious it is. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james-2-commentary

**v. 12**
- Wesley: "the law that gives freedom" is the gospel, the law of universal love, "which alone is perfect freedom." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/james/2.htm
- Ellicott notes the phrase occurs only here and in 1:25. He sees James returning to his warning about the tongue (1:26). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/2.htm
- Church Pulpit Commentary: law alone becomes bondage and liberty alone becomes lawlessness. Christianity joins the two. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/james-2.html

**v. 13**
- Wesley: at the judgment, God's mercy to believers will match the mercy they showed, and will win out over judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/james/2.htm
- Ellicott links this to the parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/2.htm

**v. 14**
- Guzik: James doesn't contradict Paul (Ephesians 2:9). He explains what *kind* of faith saves, which is faith that has works with it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-2/
- Wesley and JFB stress the word "claims": the issue is someone who *says* he has faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/james/2.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/james-2.html
- Gill: this is a bare "historical" faith or a profession of faith only, like Simon Magus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/2.htm
- Precept Austin, citing Hughes: Paul is talking about the time before conversion, James about life after it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_214-17

**vv. 15–16**
- Guzik: failing at the simplest good work shows the faith isn't alive. He warns against using religious words in place of real help. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-2/
- The Pulpit Commentary: kind words with no help harm both people. They can sour the needy person, and they damage the false sympathiser's own soul (compare 1 John 3:16–18). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/james-2.html

**v. 17**
- Wesley: such faith is "a mere dead, empty notion," as useless as telling a naked person to be clothed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/james-2.html
- Gill, following Ames: works don't give faith its life. They flow from a faith that is already alive. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-2.html
- Guzik: faith alone saves, but it has to be a living faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-2/

**v. 18**
- Guzik: James rejects the idea that some Christians have a "gift of works" and others a "gift of faith." Faith can't be seen, but works can. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-2/
- Constable: James uses the standard debating style of answering an imagined objector, as Paul also does. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/james-2.html
- Gill reads the challenge as sarcasm: James asks the boaster to do the impossible. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-2.html

**v. 19**
- Wesley: this is the same faith the devils have, and they tremble because they expect eternal torment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/james-2.html
- Guzik: demons accept that God exists, but that is not saving faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-2/
- The Pulpit Commentary, citing Lightfoot: the faith being boasted of here is the basic creed of the Jewish law ("God is one"), not the gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/2.htm

**v. 20**
- Wesley: "foolish" means empty of all goodness. Faith without works isn't really faith at all, just as a corpse isn't really a man. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/james-2.html
- Precept Austin: such faith does nothing toward salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_218-20
- Constable reads it differently; see Part 2.

**v. 21**
- Guzik: Abraham was justified by faith long before this (Genesis 15:6). Offering Isaac *showed* that his trust was real. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-2/
- JFB: Abraham was justified by works "evidentially, and before men." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/james-2.html
- How Wesley explains this is covered in Part 2.

**v. 22**
- Wesley: faith gives rise to works and is then perfected by them. Works don't give faith its existence, only its full growth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/james-2.html
- Guzik: Abraham's faith and works cooperated, and his obedience proved his faith true. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-2/
- Maclaren: James traces Abraham's sacrifice back to the faith that worked with it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/maclaren_on_james_2

**v. 23**
- Wesley: Genesis 15:6 came true twice, when Abraham first believed (Paul's focus) and when he offered Isaac (James's focus). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/james-2.html
- JFB: James means by "works" what Paul means by "faith," but fully grown rather than as a seed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/james-2.html
- Maclaren: the earlier words became true in a fuller sense once the sacrifice had perfected Abraham's faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/maclaren_on_james_2

**v. 24**
- Guzik: the "faith alone" that fails to justify is a dead faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-2/
- Precept Austin, citing Grudem: James means a person is shown to be righteous by works. Citing Moo: in Paul, "justify" is about how a relationship with God begins; in James, it is about what that relationship must look like to receive God's final approval. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_224-26
- Precept Austin, citing MacArthur: James is dealing with the evidence of salvation, not the means of it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60653/
- Ellicott: James means practical goodness, not "works of the law," and uses "justification" in a moral sense rather than a legal ("forensic") one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/2.htm

**v. 25**
- Wesley: after Abraham, father of the Jews, James names a Gentile woman and a sinner. This shows true faith produces works in every nation and in both sexes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/james-2.html
- Precept Austin cites Calvin: James chose two very different people so that no one, of any class, would think they could be counted righteous without good works. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60653/
- Precept Austin cites Guzik: James may also be gently rebuking Jewish believers' bias against Gentiles. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_224-26
- Ellicott: James put lowly Rahab beside Abraham, the great Friend of God, so his appeal would reach people of every rank. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/2.htm

**v. 26**
- Precept Austin, citing Hiebert: we might expect faith to be compared to the spirit, but James compares faith to the body. The single point is that without the second part, there is death. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_224-26
- Church Pulpit Commentary: James is aiming at people who give the faith only mental agreement. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/james-2.html

## Part 2: Where traditions differ

**v. 5: God's choosing**
- Gill (Baptist, Calvinist): the poor were chosen *to be* rich in faith, not chosen *because of* their faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/2.htm
- Wesley (Methodist): the people God chose are "generally speaking" poor in this world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/james/2.htm
- Ellicott (Anglican): God does choose, but this passage gives the reason for the choice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/james-2.html

**v. 10: kinds of sin**
- Gill says there are greater and lesser sins, but none are "venial" as opposed to "mortal," because the wages of every sin is death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/2.htm

**vv. 14–24: how James fits with Paul**
- **Methodist (Wesley):** they mean different justifications. In Paul's sense Abraham was *counted* righteous by faith before any works. In James's sense he was *made* righteous by works that came after faith. James's justification is the fruit of Paul's. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/james-2.html
  - Wesley also says James was refuting people who twisted Paul, not Paul himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/james/2.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** James means faith shown to be real before *people*, while Paul means being right before *God*. He also suggests Paul may mean justification begun and James justification completed: faith alone puts us into a justified state, and works come in "for the completing of our justification at the last great day." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jam/Jam_002.cfm
- **Reformed/evangelical "works are the evidence" view (Grudem, MacArthur, JFB, Precept Austin):** justified by works means *shown* to be justified. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_224-26 ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/james-2.html
- **"Free Grace" view (Constable):** "dead" means *useless*, not *absent*. James is not saying someone with dead faith is unsaved, and he never questions whether his readers are saved. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/james-2.html
  - Precept Austin takes the opposite line: faith without works "will end in eternal punishment." https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60653/
- **Lutheran:** I only found a secondhand note, in Remmers's overview of James hosted on StudyLight. It says Luther called James an "epistle of straw," mainly because its teaching on justification seemed to clash with Paul (compare 2:21 with Romans 3:28). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/james.html

## Part 3: Other views (only what I found)

**Scholarly debate (as reported by the Pulpit Commentary)**
- Some scholars think James was attacking Paul's teaching, or a twisted version of it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/james-2.html
- Bishop Lightfoot argued the two wrote independently. Clement of Rome combined their teaching and showed no awareness that they disagreed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/2.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary also asks whether the Judaizers of Acts 15 may have drawn a false conclusion from v. 10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/2.htm

**Not found:** Catholic, Orthodox, NET Bible, Bible Odyssey and prosperity or hyper-grace sources. Pages to look at next: catholic.com and newadvent.org on James 2:24, netbible.org notes on 2:1 and 2:24, 1517.org and lcms.org on Luther and James, and gotquestions.org on 2:5 and prosperity teaching.
